title: Jeremiah’s alphabetic laments in four cycles
english: Jeremiah, the people having been taken captive and being in Babylon, laments the city and the country and the people for what has befallen them; and he laments marking off certain sections and divisions that begin next from the letters among the Hebrews. And after finishing the lament upon each letter and, upon all, the one that begins from Thau—which is the last letter of the Hebrews—he returns to Aleph and again laments; and he does this four times, going through the twenty-two letters.
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 1 lock.

title: Captivity of the contemplative soul; Christ frees captives
english: If we see the soul becoming subject to the devil or also to his angels, and simply to the hostile powers—the soul that by nature is contemplative and able to see the things that are and to attend—we will somehow understand the captivity and the one who took captive. But fleeing for refuge to Christ, who according to the prophet Isaiah proclaimed “release to captives,” we will be freed from the captivity, even if the one who took captive reaches as far as binding. For Jesus came “to lead out those bound from bonds and those sitting in darkness from a house of prison.”
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 2 lock.

title: Twenty-two books; fourfold alphabet; Symmachus and the Seventy
english: For this reason the Hebrews say the books of the old scripture are equal in number to the letters, so as to be every introduction toward knowledge of God, just as the letters are toward every wisdom for those learning. And for this reason it is quadrupled, perhaps because the elements of bodies also stand as four. And after a little: And the edition of Aquila and Theodotion is not extant in the Lamentations, but only of Symmachus and the Seventy. And again: And someone might inquire how, the title of the book being plural—“Lamentations”—he speaks this lament in the singular in the prologue. But there are several partial ones, divided by the letters, yet all are brought up into one, being brought up toward one subject, Israel.
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 3 lock.

title: The Lord wept over Jerusalem
english: Drawing near to Jerusalem the Lord “wept and said: if you too had known the things unto your peace.” “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her own brood under the wings, and you were not willing.”

title: Jeremiah’s mystical weeping and mourning
english: If then “blessed are those who weep, for they will laugh,” Jeremiah had to weep this mystical weeping and, according to “blessed are those who mourn,” mourn those worthy of being mourned.

title: People and nations: literal and anagogical
english: And the multitude of the people, as far as the wording, seems to indicate the dwelling Israelites, and the multitude of the nations, as we said before, the proselytes. But unto anagogy—since the contemplative things are more kindred to the soul and less circumstantial than the practical—the wealth of contemplations; and the multitude of the nations the large number of good deeds. And after a little: She who was multiplied with people sits alone; by casting off the bridegroom Word the bride becomes as a widow who once was filled with the aforementioned nations.
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 7 lock.

title: Jerusalem widowed of the Word; the perfect soul
english: As far as the wording it fits for Jerusalem to be understood as said with amazement because of the change unto the gloomier—sitting isolated who once was full of people—so that the isolation may be her desolation, having had as husband the living Word as protector when she followed him present and helping, but widowed and left behind by him because of the things she had sinned. And after other things: These things then toward the literal; toward the sense, Jerusalem flourishing and full of people and nations and ruling countries is the divine soul. And it is not amazing if not only a house nor a farmstead nor the village greater than this being named, nor an ordinary city, but one differing from all cities and honored beside God, is called Jerusalem—the perfect soul—greatness of notable size being thrown around her as around the greatest city by wisdom and every virtue multiplying buildings. And after a little: And just as it is possible to see Jerusalem flourishing, multiplying with people and nations and ruling in countries, so—if virtue is liable to fall—sometimes seeing her isolated and widowed and enslaved, so as even to pay tributes to the enemy who has mastered her, according to the soul of the one who has fallen from the truth.
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 8 lock.

title: Tribute to Nebuchadnezzar and his satraps
english: And what need is there also to speak concerning this—that having begun to rule countries she is enslaved to such a degree among the enemies that she always also pays tribute, doing whatever those masters command? And they command nothing useful. And perhaps for each of the things in which she stumbles here she pays some tribute to Nebuchadnezzar, who is interpreted “Settling-in and recognition of constraint”; and not only to Nebuchadnezzar, but also to his satraps.
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 9 lock.

title: She wept in the night; no comforter from those who loved her
english: Upon the first lament, the one that began from Aleph, we were able to save the wording. But upon this one what would someone say—a city being said to have wept in the night, so that the tears are upon her cheeks—unless perhaps someone will say that those named a city, who also pay tribute, have wept, having been reminded from what sort of peace and freedom into how great a slavery and humiliation they have come? How then shall we also narrate “in the night,” or that in the time of the common rest of all human beings the city, being reminded, while resting wept, and wept with the tears flowing fountain-like upon their cheeks? And the wailing was most stretched out for them and the tears flowed on, there not being even one comforting them from so many who loved them, and everyone who loved setting aside the friendship toward her and having changed into enmity. Who then, as toward the wording, are those who formerly loved her, from whom there was not one who would comfort her? Perhaps the remaining cities of Judea—loving the metropolis for this reason—in a time of distress did not encourage her.

And after a little: These things then toward the literal. If the Word, as in the things before, should be said to weep—having fallen from her own country and coming to be in Confusion—and to have a condition opposite to laughing the laugh from joy and cheerfulness, which our Lord promises will belong to those who have wept the blessed weeping, saying: “Blessed are those who weep now, for they will laugh.” And in Job also he says, “He will fill the mouth of the true ones with laughter.” And perhaps for this reason also one of the patriarchs is called Laughter. The one groaning, then—as also the apostle has made clear saying, “For indeed we who are in the tent groan, being burdened”—weeps a weeping most nourishing and benefiting the soul, toward the cheerfulness in promise.
translator_notes: GCS Orig. III Lam. fr. 10 lock.
